title: Navigation Risk Management & Electronic Flight Bags

required_knowledge_points.title: Automation Surprise, Mode Confusion, and the Disconnect Doctrine
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What is automation surprise and how do you prevent it?' Modern glass cockpits fly the airplane precisely — even if the pilot programmed the wrong thing. The autopilot will perfectly fly you into a mountain if you told it to. The Disconnect Doctrine is simple: if the autopilot does something unexpected, DISCONNECT and hand-fly. Never fight the servos.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: AUTOMATION SURPRISE: occurs when an autoflight system executes a maneuver the pilot did not anticipate, typically caused by MODE CONFUSION — the pilot believes the autopilot is in one mode (e.g., Altitude Hold) when it is actually in another (e.g., Vertical Speed). A catastrophic example: the pilot engages the autopilot in VS mode to capture an altitude. As engine performance degrades with altitude, the autopilot pitches the nose up aggressively to maintain the commanded VS. The airspeed decays toward stall. The pilot, confused by why the nose is so high, attempts to troubleshoot the system rather than flying the airplane. FLIGHT MODE ANNUNCIATOR (FMA): the ONLY reliable indicator of what the autopilot is actually doing. Located on the PFD. The pilot must monitor the FMA, NOT the physical buttons on the autopilot bezel. Buttons show what you ASKED for; the FMA shows what the system is DOING. THE DISCONNECT DOCTRINE: if the autopilot does ANYTHING unexpected, unexplained, or uncommanded: (1) Press the Autopilot Disconnect button (on the yoke). (2) Hand-fly the airplane. (3) Troubleshoot ONLY after the aircraft is stabilized. NEVER physically fight the autopilot through the controls. Overriding servos without disconnecting can trim the aircraft into an extreme out-of-trim condition — when the servos finally release, the aircraft may pitch violently. TASK HIERARCHY: Aviate → Navigate → Communicate → Program. GPS programming during critical phases (takeoff, approach) is the LAST priority.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Mode Confusion → Automation Surprise
```
Pilot thinks: autopilot in ALTITUDE HOLD (pitch manages altitude)
Actual mode: VERTICAL SPEED (pitch manages VS regardless of speed)
→ Autopilot pitches nose UP aggressively to maintain VS
→ Speed decays toward stall
→ Pilot confused → troubleshoots instead of flying
→ AUTOMATION SURPRISE → potential loss of control
```

### The Disconnect Doctrine
| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Press **AP DISCONNECT** on yoke |
| 2 | **Hand-fly** — control attitude and airspeed |
| 3 | **Troubleshoot** ONLY after aircraft stabilized |

❌ **NEVER** fight the autopilot through the controls
- Overriding servos → extreme out-of-trim condition
- When servos release → violent pitch excursion

### Task Priority Hierarchy
```
AVIATE → NAVIGATE → COMMUNICATE → PROGRAM
```
- GPS programming is ALWAYS the lowest priority
- Never program during takeoff, climb, or approach

### FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator)
- Located on PFD — shows what autopilot is **actually doing**
- Buttons on bezel show what you **asked for**
- Monitor FMA, not buttons

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'What do you do if the autopilot does something unexpected?' DISCONNECT. Don't troubleshoot. Don't fight the controls. DISCONNECT and hand-fly.

required_knowledge_points.title: Situational Awareness Degradation — The Cascade of Errors and Cognitive Tunneling
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What causes loss of situational awareness?' It's not a single catastrophic event — it's a cascade of minor distractions that consume cognitive bandwidth until the pilot stops scanning instruments and looking outside. A dropped pen, an unlatched door, a GPS submenu — any of these can trigger cognitive tunneling that leads to a banking dive.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: SITUATIONAL AWARENESS (SA) is the pilot's accurate mental model of the aircraft's current state and its projected future state. SA degrades in three phases: (1) FAILURE TO PERCEIVE — the pilot doesn't notice the fuel gauge dropping or the heading drifting. (2) FAILURE TO COMPREHEND — the pilot notices the heading drift but doesn't understand they're being pushed toward restricted airspace. (3) FAILURE TO PROJECT — the pilot understands the drift but fails to calculate that in 10 minutes, they'll violate the boundary. COGNITIVE TUNNELING: when a minor distraction (dropped pen, GPS submenu, unlatched door) consumes all cognitive bandwidth. The pilot's instrument scan collapses. They stop looking outside. Bank and pitch excursions develop unnoticed. STERILE COCKPIT: during critical phases of flight (taxi, takeoff, approach, landing, and below 10,000 ft for Part 121), non-essential conversation and activities must cease. Part 91 has no formal sterile cockpit rule, but the principle is fundamental ADM. THE CASCADE MODEL: aviation accidents rarely result from one catastrophic failure. They result from a chain of small errors, each one increasing the probability of the next. Breaking any single link in the chain prevents the accident. The pilot's defense is constant, disciplined cross-checking of instruments, navigation, and visual references to validate their mental model.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Three Phases of SA Loss
| Phase | What Happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Perceive** | Pilot doesn't notice the data | Fuel gauge dropping, heading drifting |
| **2. Comprehend** | Pilot sees data, doesn't understand threat | Notices drift but not that it leads to restricted area |
| **3. Project** | Pilot understands now but can't predict future | Knows drift exists but not that violation is 10 min away |

### Cognitive Tunneling
- Trigger: ANY minor distraction (dropped pen, GPS menu, door latch)
- Effect: all cognitive bandwidth consumed → scan collapses
- Danger: bank/pitch excursions develop **unnoticed**
- Defense: **Aviate first** — stable airplane, THEN deal with distraction

### The Cascade of Errors
```
Minor distraction → scan stops → heading drifts → altitude changes
→ pilot notices deviation → over-corrects → enters wrong airspace
→ stress increases → more errors → LOC-I or CFIT
```
- Breaking ANY link in the chain prevents the accident

### Sterile Cockpit Principle
- No non-essential activity during critical phases
- Critical phases: taxi, takeoff, approach, landing
- Part 91 has no formal rule — but the principle saves lives

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'What causes loss of situational awareness?' NOT a single big failure. It's a cascade of minor distractions that consume cognitive bandwidth until you stop scanning.

required_knowledge_points.title: Navigation System Limitations, Signal Loss, and the Troubleshooting Flow
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What are the limitations of your navigation system?' and 'What do you do when you see a NAV flag or Red X?' Every nav system has failure modes. VOR has terrain masking and the cone of confusion. GPS has spoofing, jamming, and RAIM outages. The pilot who trusts the magenta line unconditionally will fly that line into a mountain.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: VOR LIMITATIONS: line-of-sight only — terrain masks the signal. Angular accuracy degrades with distance (1° error at 60 NM = 1 NM off course). Cone of confusion directly over the station. GPS LIMITATIONS: weak signals from 12,000 miles — vulnerable to RF interference. Military GPS jamming exercises (published via NOTAMs). SPOOFING: a ground transmitter sends fake GPS signals that gradually overpower authentic signals, leading the moving map astray WITHOUT triggering a RAIM alert. Multipath error — signal bounces off wing or building before reaching antenna. RAIM outages when satellite geometry is poor. ANTENNA SHADOWING: in steep bank turns, the GPS antenna (on top of the fuselage) can lose line-of-sight to satellites. SIGNAL LOSS RECOGNITION: Analog VOR = red cross-hatched NAV flag drops over CDI. Glass panel = Red X overlay on HSI. GPS = 'LOI' (Loss of Integrity) or 'RAIM Unavailable' message. TROUBLESHOOTING FLOW: (1) AVIATE — maintain heading and altitude. (2) Check avionics circuit breakers (do NOT reset a popped breaker more than once). (3) Check frequency/waypoint. (4) Listen for Morse code (VOR). (5) Consider altitude — climbing may restore line-of-sight. FALLBACK: if signal cannot be restored, transition to dead reckoning (heading + speed + time = estimated position) and pilotage (correlate visual landmarks with sectional chart). CORRELATION NAVIGATION: continuously verify primary nav with an independent source. GPS says you're over a lake? Look out the window — is there a lake? GPS tracking a course? Tune a VOR cross-radial to verify.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Navigation System Vulnerabilities
| System | Limitation | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **VOR** | Terrain masking (line-of-sight) | Climb for better reception |
| **VOR** | Angular error at distance (1°/60NM = 1 NM) | Cross-reference with second VOR |
| **VOR** | Cone of confusion overhead | Hold heading through cone |
| **GPS** | Military jamming (NOTAMs) | Check NOTAMs preflight |
| **GPS** | Spoofing (fake signals) | Correlate with VOR/pilotage |
| **GPS** | RAIM outage (poor geometry) | Transition to backup nav |
| **GPS** | Antenna shadowing (steep banks) | Limit bank angle, reacquire |

### Signal Loss Indicators
| System | Failure Indicator |
|---|---|
| **Analog VOR** | Red NAV flag drops over CDI |
| **Glass Panel** | Red X overlay on HSI |
| **GPS** | 'LOI' or 'RAIM Unavailable' message |

### Troubleshooting Flow
```
1. AVIATE → hold heading and altitude
2. Check circuit breakers (reset ONCE only)
3. Check frequency / waypoint entered
4. Listen for Morse code (VOR)
5. Consider altitude → climb may restore LOS
6. If unresolved → TRANSITION to backup nav
```

### Backup Navigation
- **Dead Reckoning:** last known position + heading + speed + time
- **Pilotage:** correlate visual landmarks with sectional chart
- **Correlation Navigation:** always verify primary with independent source

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** If the DPE simulates a GPS failure, your FIRST action is not to troubleshoot — it's to AVIATE (hold heading and altitude). Then troubleshoot. Then transition to backup.

required_knowledge_points.title: Electronic Flight Bags — Legal Authority, Hardware Risks, and the Fallback Doctrine
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'Can you legally fly without paper charts?' Yes — AC 91-78A explicitly authorizes EFBs as a complete replacement. But the DPE also asks: 'What happens when your iPad overheats and shuts down?' The pilot without a backup plan is suddenly lost, chartless, and vulnerable.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: LEGAL AUTHORITY: AC 91-78A authorizes Part 91 operators to completely replace paper charts with EFBs (Class 1 portable or Class 2 mounted). Requirements: the EFB must display functionally equivalent information, and the database must be current. The AC does not legally mandate a backup for Part 91, but it heavily recommends one. HARDWARE VULNERABILITIES: (1) THERMAL SHUTDOWN — consumer tablets (iPad) overheat rapidly on the glare shield under direct sunlight. The greenhouse effect of the canopy accelerates heating. When the tablet reaches its thermal limit, it shuts down and cannot be used until it physically cools — often 10-15 minutes. (2) BATTERY DEPLETION — GPS tracking + bright screen drains battery rapidly. Start at 100%, use an external power source in flight. (3) SOFTWARE CRASH — apps can freeze or crash, especially during database transitions. RF INTERFERENCE: cellular and Bluetooth radios can interfere with panel-mounted avionics. Use Airplane Mode (with GPS/WiFi enabled as needed by the app). MOUNTING: a mount that fails during turbulence can send the tablet into the flight controls. AC 91-78A requires that mounted EFBs not interfere with flight control movement. THE FALLBACK DOCTRINE: Device Redundancy (second phone/tablet with same app). Panel Integration (use G1000 MFD). Paper Backup (print departure, destination, and alternate diagrams). The 'UPDATE IN THE COCKPIT' TRAP: never download chart updates while holding short — a failed or corrupted update can make the entire database inaccessible.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### EFB Legal Framework
- **AC 91-78A** authorizes EFBs as **complete replacement** for paper charts (Part 91)
- Database must be **current**
- Display must be **functionally equivalent** to paper
- Backup NOT legally required — but **heavily recommended**

### The Three Hardware Killers
| Failure Mode | Cause | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **Thermal shutdown** | Direct sun on canopy (greenhouse effect) | Keep off glare shield, use shade |
| **Battery depletion** | GPS + bright screen | Start at 100%, use external power |
| **Software crash** | App freeze, database corruption | Carry backup device |

### The Fallback Doctrine
| Strategy | Implementation |
|---|---|
| **Device redundancy** | Phone with same EFB app, fully charged |
| **Panel integration** | G1000 MFD for charts and nav |
| **Paper backup** | Print dep/dest/alt airport diagrams |

### EFB Best Practices
- ✅ Airplane Mode ON (disable cellular/Bluetooth)
- ✅ GPS enabled (needed for moving map)
- ✅ Database updated BEFORE leaving home — never at the runway
- ✅ Mount must NOT interfere with flight controls
- ✅ Treat EFB as **supplemental** — not primary flight display

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'What if your iPad shuts down?' Have a backup: second device, panel-mounted avionics, or printed charts. 'I don't have one' = poor risk management.

lesson_overview:
## Navigation Risk Management — Automation, Awareness, Failures, and EFBs

This lesson covers the risk management dimension of modern navigation: how automation can deceive you, how awareness degrades, what happens when navigation systems fail, and how to manage the electronic flight bag that has become the center of the modern VFR cockpit.

**Automation surprise is the most insidious hazard in a glass cockpit.** The autopilot flies with precision that exceeds human capability — which means it will fly with precision into a stall if the pilot programmed the wrong mode. Mode confusion occurs when the pilot believes the autopilot is in one mode while it is actually in another. The Flight Mode Annunciator on the PFD is the only reliable indicator of what the system is doing — the physical buttons on the autopilot bezel show what the pilot asked for, which may not be what the computer is executing. The Disconnect Doctrine is absolute: if the autopilot does anything unexpected, disconnect and hand-fly. Never fight the autopilot through the controls, because overriding the servos can create an extreme out-of-trim condition that generates a violent pitch excursion when the servos finally release.

**Situational awareness does not disappear in a single dramatic moment.** It degrades through a cascade of minor distractions that individually seem harmless. A dropped pen triggers cognitive tunneling — the pilot's entire attention focuses on reaching under the seat while the aircraft slowly enters a banking turn. The instrument scan collapses. The heading drifts. The altitude changes. By the time the pilot looks up, they're disoriented and off course. The defense is the Aviate-Navigate-Communicate hierarchy: maintain aircraft control first, always, before any other task. GPS programming is the lowest-priority task in the cockpit.

**Every navigation system has failure modes that the pilot must understand and anticipate.** VOR is limited by line-of-sight physics — terrain blocks the signal, and angular accuracy degrades with distance. GPS is vulnerable to jamming (military exercises published via NOTAMs), spoofing (fake signals that lead the moving map astray without triggering alerts), and RAIM outages (insufficient satellite geometry to verify integrity). When a signal is lost, the system tells the pilot: an analog VOR drops a red NAV flag, a glass panel displays a Red X, a GPS shows a Loss of Integrity warning. The troubleshooting flow is always the same: aviate first (hold heading and altitude), then troubleshoot briefly (breakers, frequencies, identification), then transition to backup navigation (dead reckoning and pilotage) if the signal cannot be restored. Correlation Navigation — continuously verifying the primary system with an independent source — is the ongoing defense against silent failures.

**The Electronic Flight Bag has fundamentally changed VFR navigation.** AC 91-78A authorizes iPads and tablets as a complete legal replacement for paper charts in Part 91 operations. But consumer electronics are fragile instruments in an aviation environment. Direct sunlight on the glare shield can trigger thermal shutdown in minutes. GPS tracking with a bright screen drains batteries rapidly. Software crashes can lock out the entire chart database at the worst possible moment. The EFB Fallback Doctrine requires redundancy: a second device with the same app, panel-mounted avionics, or printed charts for the route. The pilot who relies on a single iPad with no backup has accepted a single point of failure for their entire navigation capability.
